title: IIT Bombay Rolls Out Wellness, Hostel and Exam Reforms After Student Suicide Row
excerpt: After weeks of protests following a student's death, the institute promises twin-sharing hostels for all years, wall-mounted fans, postponed mid-semester exams, and a student-led rewrite of invigilation rules.
body:
• IIT Bombay has rolled out a reform package spanning student wellness, hostel accommodation, mess facilities and exam procedures, in response to the death by suicide of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode on September 18.
  • Hostels get the biggest physical changes: twin-sharing rooms extended to students of all years, and ceiling fans replaced with wall-mounted fans across every hostel.
  • Exams are changing too: mid-semester tests postponed two weeks to October 10-11, and a committee with equal student representation will draft a student-friendly invigilation SOP and review the disciplinary framework before Senate approval.
  • On wellness, the institute has committed to stronger in-person counselling, mental-health sensitization for faculty and staff, a trackable grievance-redressal system, and a proposed 24x7 psychiatrist-on-call at the institute hospital — reforms students can raise through the new complaint-tracking system if deadlines slip.

The Indian Institute of Technology Bombay has announced a sweeping set of wellness, hostel and examination reforms, moving to defuse a student protest movement that followed the death by suicide of a 22-year-old student on its Powai campus last month. The measures, rolled out this week, touch nearly every part of residential campus life — from who shares a hostel room to how suspected exam malpractice is handled.

The package is the administration's answer to weeks of agitation after Sahil Wakode, a second-year Energy Science and Engineering student, was found dead in his Hostel 4 room on September 18, hours after he was allegedly caught using a mobile phone to access ChatGPT during a mid-semester exam. His parents have alleged caste-based harassment; Mumbai Police have booked invigilating professor Suryanarayana Doolla under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and the BNS abetment-to-suicide provision, and the probe has moved to the Crime Branch. The institute says no disciplinary proceedings had been initiated against Wakode.

An 18-point charter forced to the table

The reforms trace directly to a three-day student sit-in near the campus main gate that ended late on September 20, when Director Shireesh Kedare signed an 18-point charter after nearly three hours of talks, according to Education Post. The charter covers the investigation into Wakode's death alongside proposed changes to the institute's academic, disciplinary and student-welfare systems, and required the administration to deliver a written implementation plan by September 26. Notably, the director agreed to resign if the reforms are not implemented within a month.

On wellness, students had demanded a code of conduct for professors, mental-health sensitization for faculty and staff, strengthened in-person counselling with regular audits of the student-wellness centre, and 24x7 mental-health support including an on-call psychiatrist and emergency doctors. A proposed task force of students, faculty, mental-health professionals and external experts would study student distress and publish its findings. Protesters also demanded a public complaint portal, one-on-one access to the Dean's office with written replies within 18 hours, and amnesty for peaceful protesters.

"Even if students differ on the issue, we all agree on one thing: changes need to be brought in student welfare, including the wellness cell, psychiatrist support, and similar areas. Students' voices should be heard when decisions are made."

— An IIT Bombay student, speaking to PTI

Hostels: shared rooms and new fans

The most visible changes are physical. IIT Bombay currently offers twin-sharing accommodation only to first-year students; under the new model it will be extended to students of every year, a move the administration says is aimed at tackling loneliness and isolation. At the same time, the institute is replacing ceiling fans with wall-mounted fans in all hostels and utility areas — a safety intervention discussed after an earlier death in July, with batches of the new fans already arriving on campus in widely shared images.

Exams: postponed, and the rules under review

The mid-semester exams scheduled for September 26-27 were pushed to October 10-11. The delay gives a newly formed committee with equal student representation time to draft a student-friendly Standard Operating Procedure for invigilators, including step-by-step rules for handling suspected misconduct at every stage. The revised guidelines, the broader exam disciplinary framework and a complaint-tracking grievance system will go to the Senate for approval.

Criticism and what's next

The fan plan has drawn criticism. NCP (SP) spokesperson Anish Gavande questioned whether it addresses the deeper crisis, noting more than 117 students have died by suicide at IITs over the last two decades. Faculty forums have defended Professor Doolla, saying he followed prescribed procedures.

Unresolved: the Crime Branch probe continues, the Senate has yet to approve the new exam SOP, and the implementation plan is overdue against the charter's September 26 deadline. With the one-month resignation clause hanging over the director, October will show whether the promised reforms materialize or stall.
image_caption: IIT Bombay campus in Powai, Mumbai. The institute has rolled out wellness, hostel and exam reforms after the death of second-year student Sahil Wakode on September 18.
nri_angle: Thousands of diaspora families send children to IITs each year; the safety and exam reforms directly affect NRI parents weighing Indian higher education and IIT Bombay's standing as India's flagship technology institute.
